result:
The answer n = 4 is correct, and both halves of the argument hold up.

**Lower bound (n = 3 impossible).**
- For a symmetric code, distance ≥ 2 holds exactly when the single-site reduced states are the same for all codewords, so ρ^{μν} = δ_{μν} ρ.
- Diagonalizing ρ = diag(p_a) with rank r ≤ q, the slices V_{μ,a} lie in Sym²(ℂ^r) and satisfy ⟨V_{ν,a'}, V_{μ,a}⟩ = δ_{μν} δ_{aa'} p_a.
- Slices with p_a > 0 are nonzero, so the K·r slices are pairwise orthogonal. Hence K·r ≤ r(r+1)/2, so K ≤ (r+1)/2 ≤ (q+1)/2 < q for q ≥ 2.
- So no q-dimensional code exists at n = 3, and n = 2 and below are even more restrictive.

**Upper bound (n = 4 works for every q).**
- Hopping operators a_i†a_j with i ≠ j change the parity of the occupations of i and j. They therefore map the even-occupation sector to the odd sector, and every matrix element between codewords vanishes.
- Codewords have disjoint supports, so off-diagonal elements of the diagonal operators n_i also vanish.
- The diagonal elements ⟨n_i⟩ must be equal across codewords, and they are:
  - For even q, ⟨c_0|n_i|c_0⟩ = 4/q, and ⟨c_m|n_i|c_m⟩ = (2/q)·2 = 4/q because each vertex lies in exactly one matching pair.
  - For odd q, ⟨c_m|n_m|c_m⟩ = 4/q, and every other vertex lies in exactly one pair of round m, giving (2/q)·2 = 4/q.
- Normalization holds: for even q, (2/q)(q/2) = 1; for odd q, 1/q + (2/q)(q−1)/2 = 1.
- Supports are disjoint because each pair {i, j} appears in exactly one round or matching.
- This gives q orthonormal codewords, so the construction is valid.

The minimum is n = 4.
